Well, hello Doctor. I, um... I came in because, well, it’s about church. I’ve been going to the same church for, oh, must be nearly fifty years now, and I always help out with the Sunday potlucks down in the fellowship hall. I love doing it, setting everything up, making sure everyone gets a good hot plate of food. But lately, I just... I keep doing these odd things, and it’s getting folks to staring at me. 

Like just this past week, I was standing by the potluck table, right by the macaroni salad, and I picked up the serving spoon—the big heavy metal one, you know?—and I just held it up in the air. I just stood there holding it up and not moving a single inch. I don't know why, I just froze like a statue with my arm up in the air. 

And then, well, another time, I was in charge of the silverware and the napkins. They buy those nice thick paper napkins, and instead of just setting them out on the table like a normal person, I stood there folding the exact same stack of napkins over and over again. Just smoothing them down, creasing them, folding them, unfolding them, and folding them again. And there was a whole line of people just standing there, waiting on me to just hand them a napkin so they could go sit down and eat their pie, and I just kept folding that same pile. 

I just get stuck doing these strange things, Doctor, and I don't understand it. It’s terribly embarrassing, I mean, I’ve always been the one running the kitchen, I know how to serve a meal, but I just... I don't know what's happening to me. It's got me so upset I almost didn't want to show my face there this Sunday.

Well, like I was just saying about that big metal spoon and those napkins, it wasn't like I had an urge to do it. It wasn't like a sudden craving where I thought, oh, I just have to hold this spoon up. Lord, no. It was more like... well, it was exactly like you said, like my body just got stuck. 

With the spoon, my arm just went up to scoop the macaroni salad—Martha makes it with the little diced red peppers, you know, just like her mother used to do before she passed—and my arm went up, and it just... stayed. It was like the motor just cut out right in the middle of the job. I didn't decide to keep it up there. My body just froze up solid as a block of ice. And my mind, well, I was in there thinking, 'Put the spoon down, folks are waiting,' but my arm just wouldn't get the message. It was just stuck there in the air, heavy as lead.

And then with those napkins... oh, my goodness, it wasn't that I felt I needed them to be perfect or anything like that. It was more like my hands just got caught on a loop, like a broken record playing the same skip over and over. I was just folding, and folding, and smoothing that same paper napkin—they buy them in bulk from the warehouse store now, not the nice soft ones we used to have back in the nineties, so they're rough on the hands—and my fingers were just doing it all on their own. I didn't decide to keep doing it. I just couldn't seem to make them stop and do the next thing, which was handing it to Mr. Henderson who was standing right there with his slice of cherry pie just looking at me like I'd lost my marbles. 

So it's just like I told you, I keep doing these odd things at the potluck, just freezing up or repeating the same motion while folks are waiting on me, and it's not me deciding to do it at all. My body just gets entirely stuck.

Well, that's just the thing of it, Doctor. See, when my arm was up in the air with that spoon—and like I said, it was a heavy one, one of those good sturdy metal ones we've had at the church since Reverend Thomas was there, oh, must be thirty years ago now—I was standing there, frozen stiff. But my fingers just kept right on smoothing and folding. It was like my brain was shouting 'stop' and my hands were completely deaf to it. So no, even with folks telling me to stop, I just couldn't make my body mind me. It's the most helpless feeling in the world, just being trapped inside yourself while everybody watches.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, memory... yes, I suppose it is my memory, too. It's not just the names, though goodness knows I've known some of these folks since we were in pigtails and suddenly I look at them and just draw a complete blank. But mostly it's the plans, Doctor, keeping track of what I'm supposed to be doing during the week. It's gotten so bad that I've actually had to step back from my choir duties and a lot of my church volunteering. 

I used to handle the schedule for the choir robes, you see, making sure they got picked up and dropped off at the dry cleaners over on Elm Street—the one run by the Miller family, because they give the church a nice discount and they don't use that terrible heavy starch that makes the collars scratch your neck all through the sermon—but lately, I've just been getting all the plans completely mixed up. I'd forget which Sunday we needed the gold sashes and which was the purple, or I'd mix up the dates for the committee meetings and tell people the wrong time to show up, or I'd completely forget who was supposed to bring the communion bread. 

And it just... well, it makes folks uncomfortable. You can see it in their faces. They don't want to say anything harsh, bless their hearts, but I can tell they get real uneasy when I start getting the plans backwards or I show up on the wrong day entirely. And then poor Mrs. Higgins or somebody else has to come in right behind me and completely redo what I was supposed to handle in the first place. They have to make all the phone calls again and fix my messes just to make sure Sunday service goes off right. 

So I just told Pastor Davis that I need to take a step back from the choir and the organizing for a while. It just hurts my pride, Doctor, it really does, having to give up my duties and watch other people redo my work just because I can't keep a simple plan straight in my head anymore.

Well, now, let me think on that... no, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I understand folks perfectly fine. My hearing is still as sharp as it ever was, thank the Lord, and when somebody asks me a question, I know exactly what they're saying to me. And as for finding the words, oh goodness, I have plenty of words! Sometimes I think I have too many words all trying to get out the front door at the exact same time. 

It’s more like... well, like just the other day. The ladies from the church auxiliary, they were asking me about the blankets we knit for the winter charity drive, or maybe it was about the schedule for choir practice, I forget which exactly, but I understood perfectly what they wanted to know. And I mean to answer them straight, I really do. I have the answer right there in my head. But when I open my mouth, my words just decide to take a walk all on their own. 

I'll start off trying to tell them about the yarn for the blankets, but then suddenly my words just run off and I'm talking about the green beans I was snapping on the porch that morning. Mr. Henderson brought over a whole bushel from his garden, you see, the nice Kentucky Wonders that are so good for canning. And then, before you know it, I'm not talking about beans anymore, I'm going on about the hymns we sang last Sunday—like "How Great Thou Art," which is my absolute favorite, though the new piano player takes it at much too fast a tempo if you ask me—and from the hymns, I'm suddenly rambling all about my roses. I have these beautiful yellow climbing roses on the south side of the house, and they need so much pruning this time of year or they just take over the whole trellis. 

And I'll be talking and talking, going from the beans to the hymns to my roses, and I'll look up, and those poor ladies... they just have this look on their faces. Folks look at me like they completely lost the thread and they can't find what I'm saying at all. It's like they're searching for the answer about the blankets in all that chatter, and it's just gotten buried. So, no, I don't have trouble understanding them, and I know the words I want to use, but they just tumble out in this big, long river that doesn't go where it's supposed to.

I was just folding, and folding, and smoothing that same paper napkin—they buy them in bulk from the warehouse store now, not the nice soft ones we used to have back in the nineties, so they're rough on the hands—and my fingers were just doing it all on their own. I didn't decide to keep doing it. I just couldn't seem to make them stop and do the next thing, which was handing it to Mr. Henderson who was standing right there with his slice of cherry pie just looking at me like I'd lost my marbles. \n\nSo it's just like I told you, I keep doing these odd things at the potluck, just freezing up or repeating the same motion while folks are waiting on me, and it's not me deciding to do it at all. My body just gets entirely stuck.\n\nDoctor: When your arm was frozen holding the spoon up in the air, or when your hands were stuck folding those napkins, if someone had tapped you on the shoulder and said 'Stop, put it down right now,' do you think you could have forced yourself to stop and put the spoon down or put the napkins aside? Or would your body just not obey no matter how hard you tried?\n\nPatient: Well, that's just the thing of it, Doctor. See, when my arm was up in the air with that spoon—and like I said, it was a heavy one, one of those good sturdy metal ones we've had at the church since Reverend Thomas was there, oh, must be thirty years ago now—I was standing there, frozen stiff. And Mrs. Gable, she was right next to me serving the green beans. She did notice. She leaned over and she touched my arm, right here on the elbow, and she whispered, 'Mary, what on earth are you doing? Serve the macaroni.' \n\nAnd you know, I heard her clear as a bell. I wanted to put that spoon down. I was telling my arm, 'Put the spoon down, Mary, put it down right into the bowl.' But... it just wouldn't. It wouldn't obey me at all. No matter how hard I tried to force it, my arm just stayed locked up there in the air until it finally decided to come down on its own sweet time. \n\nAnd the same exact thing happened with the napkins. Mr. Henderson, bless his heart, he actually cleared his throat real loud, you know how men do when they're getting impatient, and he said, 'Mary, I just need a napkin for my pie.' He didn't tap my shoulder, but he spoke right to me, loud enough for the whole line to hear. And I tried, Doctor, I really did. I tried to just let go of that paper square and hand it over. But my fingers just kept right on smoothing and folding. It was like my brain was shouting 'stop' and my hands were completely deaf to it. So no, even with folks telling me to stop, I just couldn't make my body mind me. It's the most helpless feeling in the world, just being trapped inside yourself while everybody watches.\n\nDoctor: Mary, when did these freezing episodes and repetitive hand movements first start happening? Was it something that came on suddenly one day, or has it been gradually getting worse over weeks or months?\n\nPatient: Well, let me think on that a minute, Doctor. It certainly didn't just happen overnight, like somebody flipping a light switch, no sir. It's been... oh, I'd say right around six months now. Yes, because it was just about the time we were getting ready for the big Easter sunrise service. We always do a big breakfast after that, with the scrambled eggs and the sausage links. We don't use the patties because the links are just easier to keep warm in those metal chafing dishes they keep down in the church basement, you know, the ones with the little little fire cans underneath them. \n\nAnd that's when I first started noticing it, these little spells where my hands would just get stuck doing something odd, like I was telling you with the spoon and the napkins. But it's not just the freezing up, either, Doctor. Folks have been telling me for about that same six months that my talking has gotten all tangled up, too. They say I'm terribly hard to follow, that I just go on and on and they don't know what I'm trying to get at or what I mean. Like my sister-in-law Beatrice, she told me just the other day that she can't make heads or tails of what I'm saying half the time lately. And I don't mean to be confusing, I really don't, I just have so much on my mind and it all comes out at once, but apparently my talking has just been a mess since the spring. \n\nSo yes, I'd say it's been a good six months of this odd behavior and my talking being so hard for people to understand. Six whole months of just feeling like I'm not quite steering my own ship, and it just breaks my heart because I've always prided myself on being sharp as a tack when it comes to organizing the church meals, and now I'm just making a spectacle of myself.\n\nDoctor: Mary, besides the trouble with your speech that people have mentioned, have you noticed any changes in your memory, or do you find yourself having trouble with things like remembering names, dates, or keeping track of what you need to do during the day?\n\nPatient: Well, memory... yes, I suppose it is my memory, too. It's not just the names, though goodness knows I've known some of these folks since we were in pigtails and suddenly I look at them and just draw a complete blank. But mostly it's the plans, Doctor, keeping track of what I'm supposed to be doing during the week. It's gotten so bad that I've actually had to step back from my choir duties and a lot of my church volunteering. \n\nI used to handle the schedule for the choir robes, you see, making sure they got picked up and dropped off at the dry cleaners over on Elm Street—the one run by the Miller family, because they give the church a nice discount and they don't use that terrible heavy starch that makes the collars scratch your neck all through the sermon—but lately, I've just been getting all the plans completely mixed up. I'd forget which Sunday we needed the gold sashes and which was the purple, or I'd mix up the dates for the committee meetings and tell people the wrong time to show up, or I'd completely forget who was supposed to bring the communion bread. \n\nAnd it just... well, it makes folks uncomfortable. You can see it in their faces. They don't want to say anything harsh, bless their hearts, but I can tell they get real uneasy when I start getting the plans backwards or I show up on the wrong day entirely. And then poor Mrs. Higgins or somebody else has to come in right behind me and completely redo what I was supposed to handle in the first place. They have to make all the phone calls again and fix my messes just to make sure Sunday service goes off right. \n\nSo I just told Pastor Davis that I need to take a step back from the choir and the organizing for a while. It just hurts my pride, Doctor, it really does, having to give up my duties and watch other people redo my work just because I can't keep a simple plan straight in my head anymore.\n\nDoctor: Mary, have you noticed any weakness in your arms or legs, or do your muscles feel tight and stiff? And have you or anyone else noticed any twitching or rippling movements under your skin, especially in your arms, legs, or tongue?\n\nPatient: Well, weakness? No, Doctor, I can't say I've felt any weakness at all. My arms are still as strong as they ever were, praise the Lord. Just yesterday I was carrying in the groceries—two heavy paper sacks, mind you, because I don't like those flimsy plastic ones they use nowadays, they always tear right at the bottom the second you put canned goods in them, and I had three heavy cans of sliced peaches and a big tin of Maxwell House coffee in there—and I carried them right up the front steps without a lick of trouble. So my arms are just fine. And my legs, too. I walk down to the mailbox at the end of the driveway every single morning, rain or shine, and that's a good fifty yards down a gravel path, and my legs carry me just fine. \n\nAnd as for them feeling tight or stiff... well, no, not really. I mean, my knees might pop a little bit when I first get up out of my good armchair, the floral one in the living room that Arthur bought me for our anniversary years ago, but my muscles themselves aren't stiff or tight like you're asking. Now, when I freeze up like a statue, like I was telling you about with the spoon, well sure, I'm stuck then, but when I'm just going about my normal day and my body is listening to me, my muscles feel perfectly normal. \n\nAnd twitching? Rippling under the skin? Oh, goodness gracious, no! That sounds just awful, Doctor, like something out of one of those scary moving pictures my grandson likes to watch on the television, with bugs or something moving around inside a person. No, no, I haven't seen anything like that, and nobody else at the church or in my family has said a word about it either. My skin is just regular old lady skin, a bit thinner and more wrinkled than it used to be, maybe, but nothing is twitching or rippling underneath it, I can promise you that. \n\nAnd my tongue? No, no twitching there either. I know I told you my talking gets all tangled up and confusing for folks lately, but my tongue itself works just fine. It's not jumping around in my mouth or anything strange like that. I can still eat my peppermint hard candies and sip my hot tea without biting it or having it spasm on me. So no, Doctor, none of that twitching or weakness, none at all. It's just the freezing up and my mind getting all my plans mixed up that are giving me all this grief.\n\nDoctor: Mary, when you're talking and people say it's hard to understand you, do you have trouble finding the right words to say, or do you have trouble understanding what other people are saying to you?\n\nPatient: Well, now, let me think on that... no, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I understand folks perfectly fine. My hearing is still as sharp as it ever was, thank the Lord, and when somebody asks me a question, I know exactly what they're saying to me. And as for finding the words, oh goodness, I have plenty of words! Sometimes I think I have too many words all trying to get out the front door at the exact same time. \n\nIt’s more like... well, like just the other day. The ladies from the church auxiliary, they were asking me about the blankets we knit for the winter charity drive, or maybe it was about the schedule for choir practice, I forget which exactly, but I understood perfectly what they wanted to know. And I mean to answer them straight, I really do. I have the answer right there in my head. But when I open my mouth, my words just decide to take a walk all on their own. \n\nI'll start off trying to tell them about the yarn for the blankets, but then suddenly my words just run off and I'm talking about the green beans I was snapping on the porch that morning. Mr. Henderson brought over a whole bushel from his garden, you see, the nice Kentucky Wonders that are so good for canning. And then, before you know it, I'm not talking about beans anymore, I'm going on about the hymns we sang last Sunday—like \"How Great Thou Art,\" which is my absolute favorite, though the new piano player takes it at much too fast a tempo if you ask me—and from the hymns, I'm suddenly rambling all about my roses. I have these beautiful yellow climbing roses on the south side of the house, and they need so much pruning this time of year or they just take over the whole trellis. \n\nAnd I'll be talking and talking, going from the beans to the hymns to my roses, and I'll look up, and those poor ladies... they just have this look on their faces. Folks look at me like they completely lost the thread and they can't find what I'm saying at all. It's like they're searching for the answer about the blankets in all that chatter, and it's just gotten buried. So, no, I don't have trouble understanding them, and I know the words I want to use, but they just tumble out in this big, long river that doesn't go where it's supposed to.\n\n[Instruction]\n- Ask about exactly ONE thing. It's gotten so bad that I've actually had to step back from my choir duties and a lot of my church volunteering. \n\nI used to handle the schedule for the choir robes, you see, making sure they got picked up and dropped off at the dry cleaners over on Elm Street—the one run by the Miller family, because they give the church a nice discount and they don't use that terrible heavy starch that makes the collars scratch your neck all through the sermon—but lately, I've just been getting all the plans completely mixed up. I'd forget which Sunday we needed the gold sashes and which was the purple, or I'd mix up the dates for the committee meetings and tell people the wrong time to show up, or I'd completely forget who was supposed to bring the communion bread. \n\nAnd it just... well, it makes folks uncomfortable. You can see it in their faces. They don't want to say anything harsh, bless their hearts, but I can tell they get real uneasy when I start getting the plans backwards or I show up on the wrong day entirely. And then poor Mrs. Higgins or somebody else has to come in right behind me and completely redo what I was supposed to handle in the first place. They have to make all the phone calls again and fix my messes just to make sure Sunday service goes off right. \n\nSo I just told Pastor Davis that I need to take a step back from the choir and the organizing for a while. It just hurts my pride, Doctor, it really does, having to give up my duties and watch other people redo my work just because I can't keep a simple plan straight in my head anymore.\n\nDoctor: Mary, have you noticed any weakness in your arms or legs, or do your muscles feel tight and stiff? And have you or anyone else noticed any twitching or rippling movements under your skin, especially in your arms, legs, or tongue?\n\nPatient: Well, weakness? No, Doctor, I can't say I've felt any weakness at all. My arms are still as strong as they ever were, praise the Lord. Just yesterday I was carrying in the groceries—two heavy paper sacks, mind you, because I don't like those flimsy plastic ones they use nowadays, they always tear right at the bottom the second you put canned goods in them, and I had three heavy cans of sliced peaches and a big tin of Maxwell House coffee in there—and I carried them right up the front steps without a lick of trouble. So my arms are just fine. And my legs, too. I walk down to the mailbox at the end of the driveway every single morning, rain or shine, and that's a good fifty yards down a gravel path, and my legs carry me just fine. \n\nAnd as for them feeling tight or stiff... well, no, not really. I mean, my knees might pop a little bit when I first get up out of my good armchair, the floral one in the living room that Arthur bought me for our anniversary years ago, but my muscles themselves aren't stiff or tight like you're asking. Now, when I freeze up like a statue, like I was telling you about with the spoon, well sure, I'm stuck then, but when I'm just going about my normal day and my body is listening to me, my muscles feel perfectly normal. \n\nAnd twitching? Rippling under the skin? Oh, goodness gracious, no! That sounds just awful, Doctor, like something out of one of those scary moving pictures my grandson likes to watch on the television, with bugs or something moving around inside a person. No, no, I haven't seen anything like that, and nobody else at the church or in my family has said a word about it either. My skin is just regular old lady skin, a bit thinner and more wrinkled than it used to be, maybe, but nothing is twitching or rippling underneath it, I can promise you that. \n\nAnd my tongue? No, no twitching there either. I know I told you my talking gets all tangled up and confusing for folks lately, but my tongue itself works just fine. It's not jumping around in my mouth or anything strange like that. I can still eat my peppermint hard candies and sip my hot tea without biting it or having it spasm on me. So no, Doctor, none of that twitching or weakness, none at all. It's just the freezing up and my mind getting all my plans mixed up that are giving me all this grief.\n\nDoctor: Mary, when you're talking and people say it's hard to understand you, do you have trouble finding the right words to say, or do you have trouble understanding what other people are saying to you?\n\nPatient: Well, now, let me think on that... no, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I understand folks perfectly fine. My hearing is still as sharp as it ever was, thank the Lord, and when somebody asks me a question, I know exactly what they're saying to me. And as for finding the words, oh goodness, I have plenty of words! Sometimes I think I have too many words all trying to get out the front door at the exact same time. \n\nIt’s more like... well, like just the other day. The ladies from the church auxiliary, they were asking me about the blankets we knit for the winter charity drive, or maybe it was about the schedule for choir practice, I forget which exactly, but I understood perfectly what they wanted to know. And I mean to answer them straight, I really do. I have the answer right there in my head. But when I open my mouth, my words just decide to take a walk all on their own. \n\nI'll start off trying to tell them about the yarn for the blankets, but then suddenly my words just run off and I'm talking about the green beans I was snapping on the porch that morning. Mr. Henderson brought over a whole bushel from his garden, you see, the nice Kentucky Wonders that are so good for canning. And then, before you know it, I'm not talking about beans anymore, I'm going on about the hymns we sang last Sunday—like \"How Great Thou Art,\" which is my absolute favorite, though the new piano player takes it at much too fast a tempo if you ask me—and from the hymns, I'm suddenly rambling all about my roses. I have these beautiful yellow climbing roses on the south side of the house, and they need so much pruning this time of year or they just take over the whole trellis. \n\nAnd I'll be talking and talking, going from the beans to the hymns to my roses, and I'll look up, and those poor ladies... they just have this look on their faces. So, no, I don't have trouble understanding them, and I know the words I want to use, but they just tumble out in this big, long river that doesn't go where it's supposed to.\n\nDoctor: Mary, before all of this started about six months ago—the freezing up, the trouble with your speech, and the memory problems—did you have any kind of head injury, fall, or accident? Changes in how I act? Oh, heavens, no. I am still just plain old Mary, same as I have been for seventy-one years. I haven't gone out and bought a flashy red car or started wearing bright purple hats or anything foolish like that. Lord knows, I still do everything exactly the way I always have. 

Take my baking, for instance. Just this past Tuesday, I was making my lemon pound cake for the church bake sale. That is the one we do every spring to raise money for the children's home down in the county, though this year Pastor Thomas was saying they might need to use some of the money to fix the roof on the fellowship hall because it has been leaking right over where we set up the coffee urns. Anyway, I used the exact same recipe my mother taught me when I was just a little girl, the one where you have to cream the butter and sugar for a full ten minutes by the clock. Not a minute less, or it just will not rise right. And I took it down to the church, and all the ladies told me that I always make the absolute best pound cake and that I never change a bit. 

So no, my family and my friends, they have not said a single word about me acting different or out of character. I am still polite to my neighbors, I still keep a tidy house, and I still read my Bible every night before I go to sleep. I have these beautiful yellow climbing roses on the south side of the house, and they need so much pruning this time of year or they just take over the whole trellis. \n\nAnd I'll be talking and talking, going from the beans to the hymns to my roses, and I'll look up, and those poor ladies... they just have this look on their faces. I keep doing these odd things, and it’s getting folks to staring at me. \n\nLike just this past week, I was standing by the potluck table, right by the macaroni salad, and I picked up the serving spoon—the big heavy metal one, you know?—and I just held it up in the air. I just stood there holding it up and not moving a single inch. I don't know why, I just froze like a statue with my arm up in the air. \n\nAnd then, well, another time, I was in charge of the silverware and the napkins. They buy those nice thick paper napkins, and instead of just setting them out on the table like a normal person, I stood there folding the exact same stack of napkins over and over again. Just smoothing them down, creasing them, folding them, unfolding them, and folding them again. And there was a whole line of people just standing there, waiting on me to just hand them a napkin so they could go sit down and eat their pie, and I just kept folding that same pile. \n\nI just get stuck doing these strange things, Doctor, and I don't understand it. It’s terribly embarrassing, I mean, I’ve always been the one running the kitchen, I know how to serve a meal, but I just... I don't know what's happening to me. It's got me so upset I almost didn't want to show my face there this Sunday.\n\nDoctor: When you were holding the serving spoon up in the air and folding those napkins over and over, did it feel like something you had to do, like an urge or a compulsion you couldn't resist? Or did it feel more like your body was just stuck or frozen in that position without you consciously deciding to keep doing it?\n\nPatient: Well, like I was just saying about that big metal spoon and those napkins, it wasn't like I had an urge to do it. It wasn't like a sudden craving where I thought, oh, I just have to hold this spoon up. Lord, no. It was more like... well, it was exactly like you said, like my body just got stuck. \n\nWith the spoon, my arm just went up to scoop the macaroni salad—Martha makes it with the little diced red peppers, you know, just like her mother used to do before she passed—and my arm went up, and it just... stayed. It was like the motor just cut out right in the middle of the job. I didn't decide to keep it up there. My body just froze up solid as a block of ice. And my mind, well, I was in there thinking, 'Put the spoon down, folks are waiting,' but my arm just wouldn't get the message. It was just stuck there in the air, heavy as lead.\n\nAnd then with those napkins... oh, my goodness, it wasn't that I felt I needed them to be perfect or anything like that. It was more like my hands just got caught on a loop, like a broken record playing the same skip over and over. I was just folding, and folding, and smoothing that same paper napkin—they buy them in bulk from the warehouse store now, not the nice soft ones we used to have back in the nineties, so they're rough on the hands—and my fingers were just doing it all on their own. I didn't decide to keep doing it. I just couldn't seem to make them stop and do the next thing, which was handing it to Mr. Henderson who was standing right there with his slice of cherry pie just looking at me like I'd lost my marbles. \n\nSo it's just like I told you, I keep doing these odd things at the potluck, just freezing up or repeating the same motion while folks are waiting on me, and it's not me deciding to do it at all. My body just gets entirely stuck.\n\nDoctor: When your arm was frozen holding the spoon up in the air, or when your hands were stuck folding those napkins, if someone had tapped you on the shoulder and said 'Stop, put it down right now,' do you think you could have forced yourself to stop and put the spoon down or put the napkins aside? Or would your body just not obey no matter how hard you tried?\n\nPatient: Well, that's just the thing of it, Doctor. See, when my arm was up in the air with that spoon—and like I said, it was a heavy one, one of those good sturdy metal ones we've had at the church since Reverend Thomas was there, oh, must be thirty years ago now—I was standing there, frozen stiff. And Mrs. Gable, she was right next to me serving the green beans. She did notice. She leaned over and she touched my arm, right here on the elbow, and she whispered, 'Mary, what on earth are you doing? Serve the macaroni.' \n\nAnd you know, I heard her clear as a bell. I wanted to put that spoon down. I was telling my arm, 'Put the spoon down, Mary, put it down right into the bowl.' But... it just wouldn't. It wouldn't obey me at all. No matter how hard I tried to force it, my arm just stayed locked up there in the air until it finally decided to come down on its own sweet time. \n\nAnd the same exact thing happened with the napkins. Mr. Henderson, bless his heart, he actually cleared his throat real loud, you know how men do when they're getting impatient, and he said, 'Mary, I just need a napkin for my pie.' He didn't tap my shoulder, but he spoke right to me, loud enough for the whole line to hear. And I tried, Doctor, I really did. I tried to just let go of that paper square and hand it over. But my fingers just kept right on smoothing and folding. It was like my brain was shouting 'stop' and my hands were completely deaf to it. So no, even with folks telling me to stop, I just couldn't make my body mind me. It's the most helpless feeling in the world, just being trapped inside yourself while everybody watches.\n\nDoctor: Mary, when did these freezing episodes and repetitive hand movements first start happening? Was it something that came on suddenly one day, or has it been gradually getting worse over weeks or months?\n\nPatient: Well, let me think on that a minute, Doctor. It certainly didn't just happen overnight, like somebody flipping a light switch, no sir. It's been... oh, I'd say right around six months now. Yes, because it was just about the time we were getting ready for the big Easter sunrise service. We always do a big breakfast after that, with the scrambled eggs and the sausage links. We don't use the patties because the links are just easier to keep warm in those metal chafing dishes they keep down in the church basement, you know, the ones with the little little fire cans underneath them. \n\nAnd that's when I first started noticing it, these little spells where my hands would just get stuck doing something odd, like I was telling you with the spoon and the napkins. They say I'm terribly hard to follow, that I just go on and on and they don't know what I'm trying to get at or what I mean. Like my sister-in-law Beatrice, she told me just the other day that she can't make heads or tails of what I'm saying half the time lately. And I don't mean to be confusing, I really don't, I just have so much on my mind and it all comes out at once, but apparently my talking has just been a mess since the spring. \n\nSo yes, I'd say it's been a good six months of this odd behavior and my talking being so hard for people to understand. Six whole months of just feeling like I'm not quite steering my own ship, and it just breaks my heart because I've always prided myself on being sharp as a tack when it comes to organizing the church meals, and now I'm just making a spectacle of myself.\n\nDoctor: Mary, besides the trouble with your speech that people have mentioned, have you noticed any changes in your memory, or do you find yourself having trouble with things like remembering names, dates, or keeping track of what you need to do during the day?\n\nPatient: Well, memory... yes, I suppose it is my memory, too. It's not just the names, though goodness knows I've known some of these folks since we were in pigtails and suddenly I look at them and just draw a complete blank. But mostly it's the plans, Doctor, keeping track of what I'm supposed to be doing during the week. It's gotten so bad that I've actually had to step back from my choir duties and a lot of my church volunteering. \n\nI used to handle the schedule for the choir robes, you see, making sure they got picked up and dropped off at the dry cleaners over on Elm Street—the one run by the Miller family, because they give the church a nice discount and they don't use that terrible heavy starch that makes the collars scratch your neck all through the sermon—but lately, I've just been getting all the plans completely mixed up. I'd forget which Sunday we needed the gold sashes and which was the purple, or I'd mix up the dates for the committee meetings and tell people the wrong time to show up, or I'd completely forget who was supposed to bring the communion bread. \n\nAnd it just... well, it makes folks uncomfortable. You can see it in their faces. They don't want to say anything harsh, bless their hearts, but I can tell they get real uneasy when I start getting the plans backwards or I show up on the wrong day entirely. And then poor Mrs. Higgins or somebody else has to come in right behind me and completely redo what I was supposed to handle in the first place. They have to make all the phone calls again and fix my messes just to make sure Sunday service goes off right. \n\nSo I just told Pastor Davis that I need to take a step back from the choir and the organizing for a while. It just hurts my pride, Doctor, it really does, having to give up my duties and watch other people redo my work just because I can't keep a simple plan straight in my head anymore.\n\nDoctor: Mary, have you noticed any weakness in your arms or legs, or do your muscles feel tight and stiff? And have you or anyone else noticed any twitching or rippling movements under your skin, especially in your arms, legs, or tongue?\n\nPatient: Well, weakness? No, Doctor, I can't say I've felt any weakness at all. My arms are still as strong as they ever were, praise the Lord. Just yesterday I was carrying in the groceries—two heavy paper sacks, mind you, because I don't like those flimsy plastic ones they use nowadays, they always tear right at the bottom the second you put canned goods in them, and I had three heavy cans of sliced peaches and a big tin of Maxwell House coffee in there—and I carried them right up the front steps without a lick of trouble. So my arms are just fine. And my legs, too. I walk down to the mailbox at the end of the driveway every single morning, rain or shine, and that's a good fifty yards down a gravel path, and my legs carry me just fine. \n\nAnd as for them feeling tight or stiff... well, no, not really. That sounds just awful, Doctor, like something out of one of those scary moving pictures my grandson likes to watch on the television, with bugs or something moving around inside a person. No, no twitching there either. I know I told you my talking gets all tangled up and confusing for folks lately, but my tongue itself works just fine. It's not jumping around in my mouth or anything strange like that. I can still eat my peppermint hard candies and sip my hot tea without biting it or having it spasm on me. So no, Doctor, none of that twitching or weakness, none at all. It's just the freezing up and my mind getting all my plans mixed up that are giving me all this grief.\n\nDoctor: Mary, when you're talking and people say it's hard to understand you, do you have trouble finding the right words to say, or do you have trouble understanding what other people are saying to you?\n\nPatient: Well, now, let me think on that... no, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I understand folks perfectly fine. My hearing is still as sharp as it ever was, thank the Lord, and when somebody asks me a question, I know exactly what they're saying to me. And as for finding the words, oh goodness, I have plenty of words! Sometimes I think I have too many words all trying to get out the front door at the exact same time. \n\nIt’s more like... well, like just the other day. But when I open my mouth, my words just decide to take a walk all on their own. \n\nI'll start off trying to tell them about the yarn for the blankets, but then suddenly my words just run off and I'm talking about the green beans I was snapping on the porch that morning. And then, before you know it, I'm not talking about beans anymore, I'm going on about the hymns we sang last Sunday—like \"How Great Thou Art,\" which is my absolute favorite, though the new piano player takes it at much too fast a tempo if you ask me—and from the hymns, I'm suddenly rambling all about my roses. I have these beautiful yellow climbing roses on the south side of the house, and they need so much pruning this time of year or they just take over the whole trellis. \n\nAnd I'll be talking and talking, going from the beans to the hymns to my roses, and I'll look up, and those poor ladies... they just have this look on their faces. Folks look at me like they completely lost the thread and they can't find what I'm saying at all. It's like they're searching for the answer about the blankets in all that chatter, and it's just gotten buried. So, no, I don't have trouble understanding them, and I know the words I want to use, but they just tumble out in this big, long river that doesn't go where it's supposed to.\n\nDoctor: Mary, before all of this started about six months ago—the freezing up, the trouble with your speech, and the memory problems—did you have any kind of head injury, fall, or accident? I never go down there in my stocking feet or those cheap little slippers they sell at the pharmacy, the ones with the smooth bottoms that just ask for a broken hip. I see ladies at the church doing that in their own homes and I just think, well, you're just inviting trouble. So no, I haven't taken any tumbles or hit my head, not once. \n\nAnd a stroke? Or some sudden sickness? No, thank the Lord. I've been right as rain in my body. I eat a good bowl of oatmeal every single morning—the real kind, mind you, not those little paper packets full of sugar and fake apples, but the slow-cooked oats on the stovetop—and I think that keeps a person strong. I haven't been to the hospital for anything sudden, haven't had any spells or strokes or anything of that nature. It's just... well, it's just this freezing up and my mind getting tangled like a ball of yarn that the cat got into. But before all this started up six months ago, no, I was perfectly fine. Oh, heavens, no. I am still just plain old Mary, same as I have been for seventy-one years. I haven't gone out and bought a flashy red car or started wearing bright purple hats or anything foolish like that. Lord knows, I still do everything exactly the way I always have. \n\nTake my baking, for instance. Just this past Tuesday, I was making my lemon pound cake for the church bake sale. No, Doctor, those are exactly the same as they ever were. I wouldn't even know how to act any other way if I tried!\n\nDoctor: Mary, when you freeze up like a statue, like with the spoon or the napkins, does it happen on both sides of your body equally, or do you find that one arm or one side of your body gets stuck more often than the other side?\n\nPatient: Both sides? Well, now, let me just picture it... it’s my whole self, really. Both sides exactly the same. It’s not like my right arm gets stuck and my left arm is free to wave hello. And have you or anyone else noticed any twitching or rippling movements under your skin, especially in your arms, legs, or tongue?\n\nPatient: Well, weakness? No, Doctor, I can't say I've felt any weakness at all. My arms are still as strong as they ever were, praise the Lord. Just yesterday I was carrying in the groceries—two heavy paper sacks, mind you, because I don't like those flimsy plastic ones they use nowadays, they always tear right at the bottom the second you put canned goods in them, and I had three heavy cans of sliced peaches and a big tin of Maxwell House coffee in there—and I carried them right up the front steps without a lick of trouble. So my arms are just fine. And my legs, too. I walk down to the mailbox at the end of the driveway every single morning, rain or shine, and that's a good fifty yards down a gravel path, and my legs carry me just fine. \n\nAnd as for them feeling tight or stiff... well, no, not really. I mean, my knees might pop a little bit when I first get up out of my good armchair, the floral one in the living room that Arthur bought me for our anniversary years ago, but my muscles themselves aren't stiff or tight like you're asking. Now, when I freeze up like a statue, like I was telling you about with the spoon, well sure, I'm stuck then, but when I'm just going about my normal day and my body is listening to me, my muscles feel perfectly normal. \n\nAnd twitching? Rippling under the skin? Oh, goodness gracious, no! That sounds just awful, Doctor, like something out of one of those scary moving pictures my grandson likes to watch on the television, with bugs or something moving around inside a person. No, no, I haven't seen anything like that, and nobody else at the church or in my family has said a word about it either. My skin is just regular old lady skin, a bit thinner and more wrinkled than it used to be, maybe, but nothing is twitching or rippling underneath it, I can promise you that. \n\nAnd my tongue? No, no twitching there either. I know I told you my talking gets all tangled up and confusing for folks lately, but my tongue itself works just fine. It's not jumping around in my mouth or anything strange like that. I can still eat my peppermint hard candies and sip my hot tea without biting it or having it spasm on me. So no, Doctor, none of that twitching or weakness, none at all. It's just the freezing up and my mind getting all my plans mixed up that are giving me all this grief.\n\nDoctor: Mary, when you're talking and people say it's hard to understand you, do you have trouble finding the right words to say, or do you have trouble understanding what other people are saying to you?\n\nPatient: Well, now, let me think on that... no, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I understand folks perfectly fine. My hearing is still as sharp as it ever was, thank the Lord, and when somebody asks me a question, I know exactly what they're saying to me. And as for finding the words, oh goodness, I have plenty of words! Sometimes I think I have too many words all trying to get out the front door at the exact same time. \n\nIt’s more like... well, like just the other day. The ladies from the church auxiliary, they were asking me about the blankets we knit for the winter charity drive, or maybe it was about the schedule for choir practice, I forget which exactly, but I understood perfectly what they wanted to know. And I mean to answer them straight, I really do. I have the answer right there in my head. But when I open my mouth, my words just decide to take a walk all on their own. \n\nI'll start off trying to tell them about the yarn for the blankets, but then suddenly my words just run off and I'm talking about the green beans I was snapping on the porch that morning. Mr. Henderson brought over a whole bushel from his garden, you see, the nice Kentucky Wonders that are so good for canning. And then, before you know it, I'm not talking about beans anymore, I'm going on about the hymns we sang last Sunday—like \"How Great Thou Art,\" which is my absolute favorite, though the new piano player takes it at much too fast a tempo if you ask me—and from the hymns, I'm suddenly rambling all about my roses. I have these beautiful yellow climbing roses on the south side of the house, and they need so much pruning this time of year or they just take over the whole trellis. \n\nAnd I'll be talking and talking, going from the beans to the hymns to my roses, and I'll look up, and those poor ladies... they just have this look on their faces. Folks look at me like they completely lost the thread and they can't find what I'm saying at all. It's like they're searching for the answer about the blankets in all that chatter, and it's just gotten buried. So, no, I don't have trouble understanding them, and I know the words I want to use, but they just tumble out in this big, long river that doesn't go where it's supposed to.\n\nDoctor: Mary, before all of this started about six months ago—the freezing up, the trouble with your speech, and the memory problems—did you have any kind of head injury, fall, or accident? Or did you ever have a stroke or any sudden illness that came on all at once?\n\nPatient: Well, a head injury? Oh, heavens no, nothing like that. I haven't fallen or bumped my head at all. I'm very, very careful on my feet, Doctor, I really am. You know, we have these wooden stairs going down to the basement where we keep the deep freezer—it's one of those big chest freezers, the old kind that lasts forever, where I keep all my put-up vegetables and the extra Sunday roasts—and those stairs can get mighty slick if you aren't paying attention. But Arthur, God rest his soul, he put a good, sturdy handrail in for me years ago, and I always make sure I'm wearing my proper shoes with the rubber grips. I never go down there in my stocking feet or those cheap little slippers they sell at the pharmacy, the ones with the smooth bottoms that just ask for a broken hip. I see ladies at the church doing that in their own homes and I just think, well, you're just inviting trouble. So no, I haven't taken any tumbles or hit my head, not once. \n\nAnd a stroke? Or some sudden sickness? No, thank the Lord. I've been right as rain in my body. I eat a good bowl of oatmeal every single morning—the real kind, mind you, not those little paper packets full of sugar and fake apples, but the slow-cooked oats on the stovetop—and I think that keeps a person strong. I haven't been to the hospital for anything sudden, haven't had any spells or strokes or anything of that nature. It's just... well, it's just this freezing up and my mind getting tangled like a ball of yarn that the cat got into. But before all this started up six months ago, no, I was perfectly fine. Not a single accident or sudden illness to speak of.\n\nDoctor: Mary, besides the freezing up and the trouble keeping your thoughts organized, have you noticed any changes in your personality or the way you act? For instance, do you find yourself doing things that are out of character for you, or acting in ways that your family or friends have said seem unlike the old Mary?\n\nPatient: Changes in how I act? Oh, heavens, no. I am still just plain old Mary, same as I have been for seventy-one years. I haven't gone out and bought a flashy red car or started wearing bright purple hats or anything foolish like that. Lord knows, I still do everything exactly the way I always have. \n\nTake my baking, for instance. Just this past Tuesday, I was making my lemon pound cake for the church bake sale. That is the one we do every spring to raise money for the children's home down in the county, though this year Pastor Thomas was saying they might need to use some of the money to fix the roof on the fellowship hall because it has been leaking right over where we set up the coffee urns. Anyway, I used the exact same recipe my mother taught me when I was just a little girl, the one where you have to cream the butter and sugar for a full ten minutes by the clock. Not a minute less, or it just will not rise right. And I took it down to the church, and all the ladies told me that I always make the absolute best pound cake and that I never change a bit. \n\nSo no, my family and my friends, they have not said a single word about me acting different or out of character. I am still polite to my neighbors, I still keep a tidy house, and I still read my Bible every night before I go to sleep. It is really just... well, just that awful freezing up like a statue, and my words getting themselves all tangled up like I told you. But my heart and my personality? No, Doctor, those are exactly the same as they ever were. I wouldn't even know how to act any other way if I tried!\n\nDoctor: Mary, when you freeze up like a statue, like with the spoon or the napkins, does it happen on both sides of your body equally, or do you find that one arm or one side of your body gets stuck more often than the other side?\n\nPatient: Both sides? Well, now, let me just picture it... it’s my whole self, really. Both sides exactly the same. It’s not like my right arm gets stuck and my left arm is free to wave hello. No, it’s my whole entire body that just stops. And you know, Doctor, that right there is exactly the reason I finally decided I needed to come in and see you. I just kept doing these odd things at church, and I couldn't hide it from the congregation anymore. \n\nLike you said, with the spoon and the napkins. I'll be standing right there by the potluck table—usually I'm the one in charge of dishing out the potato salad, because everyone knows I make it with the sweet relish instead of the dill, which is exactly how Pastor Thomas prefers it—and I'll have that big metal serving spoon raised right up in the air, getting ready to put a scoop on someone's paper plate, and I just stop. I wanted to put that spoon down. I was telling my arm, 'Put the spoon down, Mary, put it down right into the bowl.' But... it just wouldn't. It wouldn't obey me at all. No matter how hard I tried to force it, my arm just stayed locked up there in the air until it finally decided to come down on its own sweet time. \n\nAnd the same exact thing happened with the napkins. Mr. Henderson, bless his heart, he actually cleared his throat real loud, you know how men do when they're getting impatient, and he said, 'Mary, I just need a napkin for my pie.' He didn't tap my shoulder, but he spoke right to me, loud enough for the whole line to hear. And I tried, Doctor, I really did. I tried to just let go of that paper square and hand it over. But my fingers just kept right on smoothing and folding. It was like my brain was shouting 'stop' and my hands were completely deaf to it. So no, even with folks telling me to stop, I just couldn't make my body mind me. It's the most helpless feeling in the world, just being trapped inside yourself while everybody watches.\n\nDoctor: Mary, when did these freezing episodes and repetitive hand movements first start happening? Was it something that came on suddenly one day, or has it been gradually getting worse over weeks or months?\n\nPatient: Well, let me think on that a minute, Doctor. It certainly didn't just happen overnight, like somebody flipping a light switch, no sir. It's been... oh, I'd say right around six months now. Yes, because it was just about the time we were getting ready for the big Easter sunrise service. We always do a big breakfast after that, with the scrambled eggs and the sausage links. We don't use the patties because the links are just easier to keep warm in those metal chafing dishes they keep down in the church basement, you know, the ones with the little little fire cans underneath them. \n\nAnd that's when I first started noticing it, these little spells where my hands would just get stuck doing something odd, like I was telling you with the spoon and the napkins. But it's not just the freezing up, either, Doctor. Folks have been telling me for about that same six months that my talking has gotten all tangled up, too. They say I'm terribly hard to follow, that I just go on and on and they don't know what I'm trying to get at or what I mean. Like my sister-in-law Beatrice, she told me just the other day that she can't make heads or tails of what I'm saying half the time lately. And I don't mean to be confusing, I really don't, I just have so much on my mind and it all comes out at once, but apparently my talking has just been a mess since the spring. \n\nSo yes, I'd say it's been a good six months of this odd behavior and my talking being so hard for people to understand. Six whole months of just feeling like I'm not quite steering my own ship, and it just breaks my heart because I've always prided myself on being sharp as a tack when it comes to organizing the church meals, and now I'm just making a spectacle of myself.\n\nDoctor: Mary, besides the trouble with your speech that people have mentioned, have you noticed any changes in your memory, or do you find yourself having trouble with things like remembering names, dates, or keeping track of what you need to do during the day?\n\nPatient: Well, memory... yes, I suppose it is my memory, too. It's not just the names, though goodness knows I've known some of these folks since we were in pigtails and suddenly I look at them and just draw a complete blank. But mostly it's the plans, Doctor, keeping track of what I'm supposed to be doing during the week. It's gotten so bad that I've actually had to step back from my choir duties and a lot of my church volunteering. \n\nI used to handle the schedule for the choir robes, you see, making sure they got picked up and dropped off at the dry cleaners over on Elm Street—the one run by the Miller family, because they give the church a nice discount and they don't use that terrible heavy starch that makes the collars scratch your neck all through the sermon—but lately, I've just been getting all the plans completely mixed up. I'd forget which Sunday we needed the gold sashes and which was the purple, or I'd mix up the dates for the committee meetings and tell people the wrong time to show up, or I'd completely forget who was supposed to bring the communion bread. \n\nAnd it just... well, it makes folks uncomfortable. You can see it in their faces. They don't want to say anything harsh, bless their hearts, but I can tell they get real uneasy when I start getting the plans backwards or I show up on the wrong day entirely. And then poor Mrs. Higgins or somebody else has to come in right behind me and completely redo what I was supposed to handle in the first place. They have to make all the phone calls again and fix my messes just to make sure Sunday service goes off right. \n\nSo I just told Pastor Davis that I need to take a step back from the choir and the organizing for a while. It just hurts my pride, Doctor, it really does, having to give up my duties and watch other people redo my work just because I can't keep a simple plan straight in my head anymore.\n\nDoctor: Mary, have you noticed any weakness in your arms or legs, or do your muscles feel tight and stiff? And have you or anyone else noticed any twitching or rippling movements under your skin, especially in your arms, legs, or tongue?\n\nPatient: Well, weakness? No, Doctor, I can't say I've felt any weakness at all. My arms are still as strong as they ever were, praise the Lord. Just yesterday I was carrying in the groceries—two heavy paper sacks, mind you, because I don't like those flimsy plastic ones they use nowadays, they always tear right at the bottom the second you put canned goods in them, and I had three heavy cans of sliced peaches and a big tin of Maxwell House coffee in there—and I carried them right up the front steps without a lick of trouble. So my arms are just fine. And my legs, too. I walk down to the mailbox at the end of the driveway every single morning, rain or shine, and that's a good fifty yards down a gravel path, and my legs carry me just fine. \n\nAnd as for them feeling tight or stiff... well, no, not really. I mean, my knees might pop a little bit when I first get up out of my good armchair, the floral one in the living room that Arthur bought me for our anniversary years ago, but my muscles themselves aren't stiff or tight like you're asking. Now, when I freeze up like a statue, like I was telling you about with the spoon, well sure, I'm stuck then, but when I'm just going about my normal day and my body is listening to me, my muscles feel perfectly normal. \n\nAnd twitching? Rippling under the skin? Oh, goodness gracious, no! That sounds just awful, Doctor, like something out of one of those scary moving pictures my grandson likes to watch on the television, with bugs or something moving around inside a person. No, no, I haven't seen anything like that, and nobody else at the church or in my family has said a word about it either. My skin is just regular old lady skin, a bit thinner and more wrinkled than it used to be, maybe, but nothing is twitching or rippling underneath it, I can promise you that. \n\nAnd my tongue? No, no twitching there either. I know I told you my talking gets all tangled up and confusing for folks lately, but my tongue itself works just fine. It's not jumping around in my mouth or anything strange like that. I can still eat my peppermint hard candies and sip my hot tea without biting it or having it spasm on me. So no, Doctor, none of that twitching or weakness, none at all. It's just the freezing up and my mind getting all my plans mixed up that are giving me all this grief.\n\nDoctor: Mary, when you're talking and people say it's hard to understand you, do you have trouble finding the right words to say, or do you have trouble understanding what other people are saying to you?\n\nPatient: Well, now, let me think on that... no, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I understand folks perfectly fine. My hearing is still as sharp as it ever was, thank the Lord, and when somebody asks me a question, I know exactly what they're saying to me. And as for finding the words, oh goodness, I have plenty of words! Sometimes I think I have too many words all trying to get out the front door at the exact same time. \n\nIt’s more like... well, like just the other day. The ladies from the church auxiliary, they were asking me about the blankets we knit for the winter charity drive, or maybe it was about the schedule for choir practice, I forget which exactly, but I understood perfectly what they wanted to know. And I mean to answer them straight, I really do. I have the answer right there in my head. Mr. Henderson brought over a whole bushel from his garden, you see, the nice Kentucky Wonders that are so good for canning. And then, before you know it, I'm not talking about beans anymore, I'm going on about the hymns we sang last Sunday—like \"How Great Thou Art,\" which is my absolute favorite, though the new piano player takes it at much too fast a tempo if you ask me—and from the hymns, I'm suddenly rambling all about my roses. I have these beautiful yellow climbing roses on the south side of the house, and they need so much pruning this time of year or they just take over the whole trellis. \n\nAnd I'll be talking and talking, going from the beans to the hymns to my roses, and I'll look up, and those poor ladies... they just have this look on their faces. Folks look at me like they completely lost the thread and they can't find what I'm saying at all. It's like they're searching for the answer about the blankets in all that chatter, and it's just gotten buried. So, no, I don't have trouble understanding them, and I know the words I want to use, but they just tumble out in this big, long river that doesn't go where it's supposed to.\n\nDoctor: Mary, before all of this started about six months ago—the freezing up, the trouble with your speech, and the memory problems—did you have any kind of head injury, fall, or accident? Or did you ever have a stroke or any sudden illness that came on all at once?\n\nPatient: Well, a head injury? Oh, heavens no, nothing like that. I haven't fallen or bumped my head at all. I'm very, very careful on my feet, Doctor, I really am. I wouldn't even know how to act any other way if I tried!\n\nDoctor: Mary, when you freeze up like a statue, like with the spoon or the napkins, does it happen on both sides of your body equally, or do you find that one arm or one side of your body gets stuck more often than the other side?\n\nPatient: Both sides? ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Oh, the words come to me just fine, Doctor. Heavens, I don't have any trouble finding words at all, it's not like my mind forgets what a thing is called. I have plenty of words, maybe too many! It's just exactly like you said, they come out but they just keep going and going and going, and I can't seem to rein them back in. 

I really do mean to answer straight! Just last Wednesday, for example, the ladies at the church were asking me about choir practice, and then Mrs. Higgins asked how that cross-stitch blanket was coming along for my great-niece—the one due in August, you remember I told you about her. And I meant to just give a simple answer. I meant to just say that the blanket was coming along fine and we were going to practice the special anthem for Sunday. But before I knew it, my words just ran off entirely on their own. 

I started talking about the blanket, and then somehow I was going on about the green beans I was canning last summer, because I always use the big pressure cooker for those and you have to be so careful with the seal on the lid. And then that just rolled right into talking about the hymns we sang last Sunday, because we sang "How Great Thou Art" and it's always been my absolute favorite since I was a little girl in Sunday school. And from the hymns, well, I went straight on to talking about my roses out by the front porch. I have these beautiful yellow climbing roses, you see, but the Japanese beetles have been just terrible this year, eating the leaves right down to the veins, and I was explaining all about the soapy water spray I use on them. 

And I was just talking and talking, running right off from the beans to the hymns to my roses, and I couldn't stop myself from saying all those other things even though I knew it wasn't what they asked me. And I looked at the ladies, and they were just staring at me. Folks look at me like they can't find what I'm saying, like they're trying to follow the path but I've gone and wandered off into the woods. It's terribly frustrating, because the words are all perfectly good words, they just refuse to stay in the order I meant to put them in.

They have to make all the phone calls again and fix my messes just to make sure Sunday service goes off right. \n\nSo I just told Pastor Davis that I need to take a step back from the choir and the organizing for a while. It just hurts my pride, Doctor, it really does, having to give up my duties and watch other people redo my work just because I can't keep a simple plan straight in my head anymore.\n\nDoctor: Mary, have you noticed any weakness in your arms or legs, or do your muscles feel tight and stiff? And have you or anyone else noticed any twitching or rippling movements under your skin, especially in your arms, legs, or tongue?\n\nPatient: Well, weakness? No, Doctor, I can't say I've felt any weakness at all. My arms are still as strong as they ever were, praise the Lord. Just yesterday I was carrying in the groceries—two heavy paper sacks, mind you, because I don't like those flimsy plastic ones they use nowadays, they always tear right at the bottom the second you put canned goods in them, and I had three heavy cans of sliced peaches and a big tin of Maxwell House coffee in there—and I carried them right up the front steps without a lick of trouble. So my arms are just fine. And my legs, too. I walk down to the mailbox at the end of the driveway every single morning, rain or shine, and that's a good fifty yards down a gravel path, and my legs carry me just fine. \n\nAnd as for them feeling tight or stiff... well, no, not really. I mean, my knees might pop a little bit when I first get up out of my good armchair, the floral one in the living room that Arthur bought me for our anniversary years ago, but my muscles themselves aren't stiff or tight like you're asking. Now, when I freeze up like a statue, like I was telling you about with the spoon, well sure, I'm stuck then, but when I'm just going about my normal day and my body is listening to me, my muscles feel perfectly normal. \n\nAnd twitching? Rippling under the skin? Oh, goodness gracious, no! That sounds just awful, Doctor, like something out of one of those scary moving pictures my grandson likes to watch on the television, with bugs or something moving around inside a person. No, no, I haven't seen anything like that, and nobody else at the church or in my family has said a word about it either. My skin is just regular old lady skin, a bit thinner and more wrinkled than it used to be, maybe, but nothing is twitching or rippling underneath it, I can promise you that. \n\nAnd my tongue? No, no twitching there either. I know I told you my talking gets all tangled up and confusing for folks lately, but my tongue itself works just fine. It's not jumping around in my mouth or anything strange like that. I can still eat my peppermint hard candies and sip my hot tea without biting it or having it spasm on me. So no, Doctor, none of that twitching or weakness, none at all. It's just the freezing up and my mind getting all my plans mixed up that are giving me all this grief.\n\nDoctor: Mary, when you're talking and people say it's hard to understand you, do you have trouble finding the right words to say, or do you have trouble understanding what other people are saying to you?\n\nPatient: Well, now, let me think on that... no, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I understand folks perfectly fine. My hearing is still as sharp as it ever was, thank the Lord, and when somebody asks me a question, I know exactly what they're saying to me. And as for finding the words, oh goodness, I have plenty of words! Sometimes I think I have too many words all trying to get out the front door at the exact same time. \n\nIt’s more like... well, like just the other day. The ladies from the church auxiliary, they were asking me about the blankets we knit for the winter charity drive, or maybe it was about the schedule for choir practice, I forget which exactly, but I understood perfectly what they wanted to know. And I mean to answer them straight, I really do. I have the answer right there in my head. But when I open my mouth, my words just decide to take a walk all on their own. \n\nI'll start off trying to tell them about the yarn for the blankets, but then suddenly my words just run off and I'm talking about the green beans I was snapping on the porch that morning. Mr. Henderson brought over a whole bushel from his garden, you see, the nice Kentucky Wonders that are so good for canning. And then, before you know it, I'm not talking about beans anymore, I'm going on about the hymns we sang last Sunday—like \"How Great Thou Art,\" which is my absolute favorite, though the new piano player takes it at much too fast a tempo if you ask me—and from the hymns, I'm suddenly rambling all about my roses. I have these beautiful yellow climbing roses on the south side of the house, and they need so much pruning this time of year or they just take over the whole trellis. \n\nAnd I'll be talking and talking, going from the beans to the hymns to my roses, and I'll look up, and those poor ladies... they just have this look on their faces. Folks look at me like they completely lost the thread and they can't find what I'm saying at all. It's like they're searching for the answer about the blankets in all that chatter, and it's just gotten buried. So, no, I don't have trouble understanding them, and I know the words I want to use, but they just tumble out in this big, long river that doesn't go where it's supposed to.\n\nDoctor: Mary, before all of this started about six months ago—the freezing up, the trouble with your speech, and the memory problems—did you have any kind of head injury, fall, or accident? Or did you ever have a stroke or any sudden illness that came on all at once?\n\nPatient: Well, a head injury? Oh, heavens no, nothing like that. I haven't fallen or bumped my head at all. I'm very, very careful on my feet, Doctor, I really am. You know, we have these wooden stairs going down to the basement where we keep the deep freezer—it's one of those big chest freezers, the old kind that lasts forever, where I keep all my put-up vegetables and the extra Sunday roasts—and those stairs can get mighty slick if you aren't paying attention. But Arthur, God rest his soul, he put a good, sturdy handrail in for me years ago, and I always make sure I'm wearing my proper shoes with the rubber grips. I never go down there in my stocking feet or those cheap little slippers they sell at the pharmacy, the ones with the smooth bottoms that just ask for a broken hip. I see ladies at the church doing that in their own homes and I just think, well, you're just inviting trouble. So no, I haven't taken any tumbles or hit my head, not once. \n\nAnd a stroke? Or some sudden sickness? No, thank the Lord. I've been right as rain in my body. I eat a good bowl of oatmeal every single morning—the real kind, mind you, not those little paper packets full of sugar and fake apples, but the slow-cooked oats on the stovetop—and I think that keeps a person strong. I haven't been to the hospital for anything sudden, haven't had any spells or strokes or anything of that nature. It's just... well, it's just this freezing up and my mind getting tangled like a ball of yarn that the cat got into. But before all this started up six months ago, no, I was perfectly fine. Not a single accident or sudden illness to speak of.\n\nDoctor: Mary, besides the freezing up and the trouble keeping your thoughts organized, have you noticed any changes in your personality or the way you act? For instance, do you find yourself doing things that are out of character for you, or acting in ways that your family or friends have said seem unlike the old Mary?\n\nPatient: Changes in how I act? Oh, heavens, no. I am still just plain old Mary, same as I have been for seventy-one years. I haven't gone out and bought a flashy red car or started wearing bright purple hats or anything foolish like that. Lord knows, I still do everything exactly the way I always have. \n\nTake my baking, for instance. Just this past Tuesday, I was making my lemon pound cake for the church bake sale. That is the one we do every spring to raise money for the children's home down in the county, though this year Pastor Thomas was saying they might need to use some of the money to fix the roof on the fellowship hall because it has been leaking right over where we set up the coffee urns. Anyway, I used the exact same recipe my mother taught me when I was just a little girl, the one where you have to cream the butter and sugar for a full ten minutes by the clock. Not a minute less, or it just will not rise right. And I took it down to the church, and all the ladies told me that I always make the absolute best pound cake and that I never change a bit. \n\nSo no, my family and my friends, they have not said a single word about me acting different or out of character. I am still polite to my neighbors, I still keep a tidy house, and I still read my Bible every night before I go to sleep. It is really just... well, just that awful freezing up like a statue, and my words getting themselves all tangled up like I told you. But my heart and my personality? No, Doctor, those are exactly the same as they ever were. I wouldn't even know how to act any other way if I tried!\n\nDoctor: Mary, when you freeze up like a statue, like with the spoon or the napkins, does it happen on both sides of your body equally, or do you find that one arm or one side of your body gets stuck more often than the other side?\n\nPatient: Both sides? Well, now, let me just picture it... it’s my whole self, really. Both sides exactly the same. It’s not like my right arm gets stuck and my left arm is free to wave hello. No, it’s my whole entire body that just stops. And you know, Doctor, that right there is exactly the reason I finally decided I needed to come in and see you. I just kept doing these odd things at church, and I couldn't hide it from the congregation anymore. \n\nLike you said, with the spoon and the napkins. I'll be standing right there by the potluck table—usually I'm the one in charge of dishing out the potato salad, because everyone knows I make it with the sweet relish instead of the dill, which is exactly how Pastor Thomas prefers it—and I'll have that big metal serving spoon raised right up in the air, getting ready to put a scoop on someone's paper plate, and I just stop. I'll be holding the serving spoon up and not moving an inch. Just frozen solid, both arms, my whole body, like I turned to stone right there in the fellowship hall. \n\nOr I'll be over at the end of the table where we keep the silverware and the cups, and I'll start folding the napkins. Last week Mrs. Higgins was right behind me, and you know she has that bad hip, she shouldn't be standing on the hard linoleum for too long, but there I was, making everyone wait because I couldn't stop folding that same stack or get my body to unfreeze and move along. \n\nSo, yes, to answer your question, it is definitely both sides at once. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Oh, no, Doctor, I don't have any trouble understanding what people mean. I hear them clear as day and I know exactly what they're getting at. Now, I know I didn't get to finish high school—I had to leave school back in the eighth grade to help my mother with the younger ones, there were six of us kids, you see, and someone had to do the washing and the cooking—but that doesn't mean I don't have a good head on my shoulders. I understand complicated things just fine! 

Why, just the other week, Pastor Thomas was giving this long, terribly complicated sermon about the metaphysical nature of grace—that was the exact word he used, metaphysical, which is a big ten-dollar word if you ask me—and he was going on and on about abstract concepts and the Holy Spirit and all sorts of deep theological things that would make some people's heads spin. But I followed every single word. I sat right there in the third pew, right next to Mrs. Higgins who was nodding off, bless her heart, and I understood exactly what he meant about grace being like a river that washes over the stones in a creek bed. 

And it's the exact same thing when I watch the evening news, with all those politicians in Washington using their fancy jargon and talking in circles about the economy and the infrastructure and whatnot. I know exactly what they're really saying, even when they try to dress it up in complicated words to confuse us everyday folks. I just sit in my armchair with my cross-stitch and I follow right along. So no, when folks talk to me, I don't get lost or confused at all. It's only my own words that run away from me and go off into the woods like I was telling you before, but my ears and my understanding work perfectly fine, always have.

Well, heavens no, Doctor, I haven't noticed anything like that at all. I've never been one to have a short temper, not now and not ever. My mother, God rest her soul, she used to say I was the most even-tempered out of all six of us kids.
