It’s that nice soft knit one I got on sale at JCPenney a few years back, the one with the little pearl buttons. 

Now, a lot of women would have pitched an absolute fit right then and there, having coffee spilled on their Sunday best, but I didn't get upset one bit. I didn't raise my voice or get irritable or snap at her. I just patted her arm and told her it was no use crying over spilled coffee, and I marched right into the ladies' room to dab it with some cold water and a paper towel before it could set into the fibers. 

So, no, I don't find myself getting frustrated or angry more easily these last six months. I might get frustrated with my own words when they won't line up, or maybe with those Japanese beetles tearing up my yellow roses, I'll give you that, because they are just a menace this year... but with people and just my everyday feelings? No, my mood is just as cheerful and steady as it's always been. I haven't changed one bit in that department.

Well, like I was just telling you a minute ago, Doctor, my sentences are put together perfectly fine. I certainly don't leave out any little words like 'the' or 'and' or 'is.' Even though I had to leave school in the eighth grade to help my mother with the washing and the younger children, she was an absolute stickler for proper grammar. She wouldn't tolerate any lazy talking or broken, half-finished sentences in her house, no sir. So my sentences come out whole and complete, exactly the way they're supposed to. 

It's just like we were just talking about, it's only the topics that get all jumbled. When the ladies at the church come up and ask me about the baby blankets—we're doing them in pastel colors this year, mostly mint greens and pale yellows for the charity drive, since you never know if a family is having a boy or a girl—or if they ask me about the choir practice, I really do mean to give them a straight, sensible answer. I have a perfectly good, grammatically correct sentence ready to go in my head! 

But then, well, my words just run off on their own again. I'll start out meaning to answer about the blankets or the choir, but then suddenly I'm talking about the pressure-cooker beans I'm making for supper, and then I'm on to the Sunday hymns we sang last week, and before you know it I'm going on about my yellow roses. 

Every single sentence is put together right, but folks just... well, they look at me like they absolutely can't find what I'm saying. They get this polite little squint, you know the look, where they're trying so hard to be nice but they are just completely lost in the woods. They hear all the words, and the grammar is right as rain, but because I jumped from the choir to the beans to the roses so fast, they just can't figure out how I got from point A to point B. So no, I don't have any trouble putting the grammar together at all, it's just those topics refusing to stay in their proper lanes.

My body just gets entirely stuck.\n\nDoctor: When your arm was frozen holding the spoon up in the air, or when your hands were stuck folding those napkins, if someone had tapped you on the shoulder and said 'Stop, put it down right now,' do you think you could have forced yourself to stop and put the spoon down or put the napkins aside? Or would your body just not obey no matter how hard you tried?\n\nPatient: Well, that's just the thing of it, Doctor. See, when my arm was up in the air with that spoon—and like I said, it was a heavy one, one of those good sturdy metal ones we've had at the church since Reverend Thomas was there, oh, must be thirty years ago now—I was standing there, frozen stiff. And Mrs. Gable, she was right next to me serving the green beans. She did notice. She leaned over and she touched my arm, right here on the elbow, and she whispered, 'Mary, what on earth are you doing? Serve the macaroni.' \n\nAnd you know, I heard her clear as a bell. I wanted to put that spoon down. I was telling my arm, 'Put the spoon down, Mary, put it down right into the bowl.' But... it just wouldn't. It wouldn't obey me at all. No matter how hard I tried to force it, my arm just stayed locked up there in the air until it finally decided to come down on its own sweet time. \n\nAnd the same exact thing happened with the napkins. Mr. Henderson, bless his heart, he actually cleared his throat real loud, you know how men do when they're getting impatient, and he said, 'Mary, I just need a napkin for my pie.' He didn't tap my shoulder, but he spoke right to me, loud enough for the whole line to hear. And I tried, Doctor, I really did. I tried to just let go of that paper square and hand it over. But my fingers just kept right on smoothing and folding. It was like my brain was shouting 'stop' and my hands were completely deaf to it. So no, even with folks telling me to stop, I just couldn't make my body mind me. It's the most helpless feeling in the world, just being trapped inside yourself while everybody watches.\n\nDoctor: Mary, when did these freezing episodes and repetitive hand movements first start happening? Was it something that came on suddenly one day, or has it been gradually getting worse over weeks or months?\n\nPatient: Well, let me think on that a minute, Doctor. It certainly didn't just happen overnight, like somebody flipping a light switch, no sir. It's been... oh, I'd say right around six months now. Yes, because it was just about the time we were getting ready for the big Easter sunrise service. We always do a big breakfast after that, with the scrambled eggs and the sausage links. We don't use the patties because the links are just easier to keep warm in those metal chafing dishes they keep down in the church basement, you know, the ones with the little little fire cans underneath them. \n\nAnd that's when I first started noticing it, these little spells where my hands would just get stuck doing something odd, like I was telling you with the spoon and the napkins. But it's not just the freezing up, either, Doctor. Folks have been telling me for about that same six months that my talking has gotten all tangled up, too. They say I'm terribly hard to follow, that I just go on and on and they don't know what I'm trying to get at or what I mean. Like my sister-in-law Beatrice, she told me just the other day that she can't make heads or tails of what I'm saying half the time lately. And I don't mean to be confusing, I really don't, I just have so much on my mind and it all comes out at once, but apparently my talking has just been a mess since the spring. \n\nSo yes, I'd say it's been a good six months of this odd behavior and my talking being so hard for people to understand. Six whole months of just feeling like I'm not quite steering my own ship, and it just breaks my heart because I've always prided myself on being sharp as a tack when it comes to organizing the church meals, and now I'm just making a spectacle of myself.\n\nDoctor: Mary, besides the trouble with your speech that people have mentioned, have you noticed any changes in your memory, or do you find yourself having trouble with things like remembering names, dates, or keeping track of what you need to do during the day?\n\nPatient: Well, memory... yes, I suppose it is my memory, too. It's not just the names, though goodness knows I've known some of these folks since we were in pigtails and suddenly I look at them and just draw a complete blank. But mostly it's the plans, Doctor, keeping track of what I'm supposed to be doing during the week. It's gotten so bad that I've actually had to step back from my choir duties and a lot of my church volunteering. \n\nI used to handle the schedule for the choir robes, you see, making sure they got picked up and dropped off at the dry cleaners over on Elm Street—the one run by the Miller family, because they give the church a nice discount and they don't use that terrible heavy starch that makes the collars scratch your neck all through the sermon—but lately, I've just been getting all the plans completely mixed up. I'd forget which Sunday we needed the gold sashes and which was the purple, or I'd mix up the dates for the committee meetings and tell people the wrong time to show up, or I'd completely forget who was supposed to bring the communion bread. \n\nAnd it just... well, it makes folks uncomfortable. You can see it in their faces. They don't want to say anything harsh, bless their hearts, but I can tell they get real uneasy when I start getting the plans backwards or I show up on the wrong day entirely. And then poor Mrs. Higgins or somebody else has to come in right behind me and completely redo what I was supposed to handle in the first place. They have to make all the phone calls again and fix my messes just to make sure Sunday service goes off right. \n\nSo I just told Pastor Davis that I need to take a step back from the choir and the organizing for a while. It just hurts my pride, Doctor, it really does, having to give up my duties and watch other people redo my work just because I can't keep a simple plan straight in my head anymore.\n\nDoctor: Mary, have you noticed any weakness in your arms or legs, or do your muscles feel tight and stiff? And have you or anyone else noticed any twitching or rippling movements under your skin, especially in your arms, legs, or tongue?\n\nPatient: Well, weakness? No, Doctor, I can't say I've felt any weakness at all. My arms are still as strong as they ever were, praise the Lord. Just yesterday I was carrying in the groceries—two heavy paper sacks, mind you, because I don't like those flimsy plastic ones they use nowadays, they always tear right at the bottom the second you put canned goods in them, and I had three heavy cans of sliced peaches and a big tin of Maxwell House coffee in there—and I carried them right up the front steps without a lick of trouble. So my arms are just fine. And my legs, too. I walk down to the mailbox at the end of the driveway every single morning, rain or shine, and that's a good fifty yards down a gravel path, and my legs carry me just fine. \n\nAnd as for them feeling tight or stiff... well, no, not really. I mean, my knees might pop a little bit when I first get up out of my good armchair, the floral one in the living room that Arthur bought me for our anniversary years ago, but my muscles themselves aren't stiff or tight like you're asking. Now, when I freeze up like a statue, like I was telling you about with the spoon, well sure, I'm stuck then, but when I'm just going about my normal day and my body is listening to me, my muscles feel perfectly normal. \n\nAnd twitching? Rippling under the skin? Oh, goodness gracious, no! That sounds just awful, Doctor, like something out of one of those scary moving pictures my grandson likes to watch on the television, with bugs or something moving around inside a person. No, no, I haven't seen anything like that, and nobody else at the church or in my family has said a word about it either. My skin is just regular old lady skin, a bit thinner and more wrinkled than it used to be, maybe, but nothing is twitching or rippling underneath it, I can promise you that. \n\nAnd my tongue? No, no twitching there either. I know I told you my talking gets all tangled up and confusing for folks lately, but my tongue itself works just fine. It's not jumping around in my mouth or anything strange like that. I can still eat my peppermint hard candies and sip my hot tea without biting it or having it spasm on me. So no, Doctor, none of that twitching or weakness, none at all. It's just the freezing up and my mind getting all my plans mixed up that are giving me all this grief.\n\nDoctor: Mary, when you're talking and people say it's hard to understand you, do you have trouble finding the right words to say, or do you have trouble understanding what other people are saying to you?\n\nPatient: Well, now, let me think on that... no, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I understand folks perfectly fine. My hearing is still as sharp as it ever was, thank the Lord, and when somebody asks me a question, I know exactly what they're saying to me. And as for finding the words, oh goodness, I have plenty of words! Sometimes I think I have too many words all trying to get out the front door at the exact same time. \n\nIt’s more like... well, like just the other day. The ladies from the church auxiliary, they were asking me about the blankets we knit for the winter charity drive, or maybe it was about the schedule for choir practice, I forget which exactly, but I understood perfectly what they wanted to know. And I mean to answer them straight, I really do. I have the answer right there in my head. But when I open my mouth, my words just decide to take a walk all on their own. \n\nI'll start off trying to tell them about the yarn for the blankets, but then suddenly my words just run off and I'm talking about the green beans I was snapping on the porch that morning. Mr. Henderson brought over a whole bushel from his garden, you see, the nice Kentucky Wonders that are so good for canning. And then, before you know it, I'm not talking about beans anymore, I'm going on about the hymns we sang last Sunday—like \"How Great Thou Art,\" which is my absolute favorite, though the new piano player takes it at much too fast a tempo if you ask me—and from the hymns, I'm suddenly rambling all about my roses. I have these beautiful yellow climbing roses on the south side of the house, and they need so much pruning this time of year or they just take over the whole trellis. \n\nAnd I'll be talking and talking, going from the beans to the hymns to my roses, and I'll look up, and those poor ladies... they just have this look on their faces. Folks look at me like they completely lost the thread and they can't find what I'm saying at all. It's like they're searching for the answer about the blankets in all that chatter, and it's just gotten buried. So, no, I don't have trouble understanding them, and I know the words I want to use, but they just tumble out in this big, long river that doesn't go where it's supposed to.\n\nDoctor: Mary, before all of this started about six months ago—the freezing up, the trouble with your speech, and the memory problems—did you have any kind of head injury, fall, or accident? Or did you ever have a stroke or any sudden illness that came on all at once?\n\nPatient: Well, a head injury? Oh, heavens no, nothing like that. I haven't fallen or bumped my head at all. I'm very, very careful on my feet, Doctor, I really am. You know, we have these wooden stairs going down to the basement where we keep the deep freezer—it's one of those big chest freezers, the old kind that lasts forever, where I keep all my put-up vegetables and the extra Sunday roasts—and those stairs can get mighty slick if you aren't paying attention. But Arthur, God rest his soul, he put a good, sturdy handrail in for me years ago, and I always make sure I'm wearing my proper shoes with the rubber grips. I never go down there in my stocking feet or those cheap little slippers they sell at the pharmacy, the ones with the smooth bottoms that just ask for a broken hip. I see ladies at the church doing that in their own homes and I just think, well, you're just inviting trouble. So no, I haven't taken any tumbles or hit my head, not once. \n\nAnd a stroke? Or some sudden sickness? No, thank the Lord. I've been right as rain in my body. I eat a good bowl of oatmeal every single morning—the real kind, mind you, not those little paper packets full of sugar and fake apples, but the slow-cooked oats on the stovetop—and I think that keeps a person strong. I haven't been to the hospital for anything sudden, haven't had any spells or strokes or anything of that nature. It's just... well, it's just this freezing up and my mind getting tangled like a ball of yarn that the cat got into. But before all this started up six months ago, no, I was perfectly fine. Not a single accident or sudden illness to speak of.\n\nDoctor: Mary, besides the freezing up and the trouble keeping your thoughts organized, have you noticed any changes in your personality or the way you act? For instance, do you find yourself doing things that are out of character for you, or acting in ways that your family or friends have said seem unlike the old Mary?\n\nPatient: Changes in how I act? Oh, heavens, no. I am still just plain old Mary, same as I have been for seventy-one years. I haven't gone out and bought a flashy red car or started wearing bright purple hats or anything foolish like that. Lord knows, I still do everything exactly the way I always have. \n\nTake my baking, for instance. Just this past Tuesday, I was making my lemon pound cake for the church bake sale. Anyway, I used the exact same recipe my mother taught me when I was just a little girl, the one where you have to cream the butter and sugar for a full ten minutes by the clock. Not a minute less, or it just will not rise right. I wouldn't even know how to act any other way if I tried!\n\nDoctor: Mary, when you freeze up like a statue, like with the spoon or the napkins, does it happen on both sides of your body equally, or do you find that one arm or one side of your body gets stuck more often than the other side?\n\nPatient: Both sides? Well, now, let me just picture it... it’s my whole self, really. Both sides exactly the same. It’s not like my right arm gets stuck and my left arm is free to wave hello. No, it’s my whole entire body that just stops. And you know, Doctor, that right there is exactly the reason I finally decided I needed to come in and see you. I just kept doing these odd things at church, and I couldn't hide it from the congregation anymore. \n\nLike you said, with the spoon and the napkins. Just frozen solid, both arms, my whole body, like I turned to stone right there in the fellowship hall. \n\nOr I'll be over at the end of the table where we keep the silverware and the cups, and I'll start folding the napkins. Both my hands just doing the same thing, caught in a loop, or freezing up entirely, while a whole line of people are just waiting on me! Last week Mrs. Higgins was right behind me, and you know she has that bad hip, she shouldn't be standing on the hard linoleum for too long, but there I was, making everyone wait because I couldn't stop folding that same stack or get my body to unfreeze and move along. \n\nSo, yes, to answer your question, it is definitely both sides at once. My eyes move right where I tell them to, up, down, side to side, no trouble at all. \n\nI mean, I do wear my bifocals, of course, but I've had to wear glasses for reading and distance since I was about forty-five years old. Dr. Henderson down at the vision center on Elm Street—he’s such a polite young man, he took over the whole practice when his father retired and moved down to Boca Raton—he always tells me my eyes are doing remarkably well for a lady of my age. If your eyes couldn't look down right, you'd make a complete mess of the whole project! So no, Doctor, my eyes don't freeze up or get stiff like the rest of me does. They dart around just as quick and easy as they ever did.\n\nDoctor: Mary, when you're talking and your words go wandering off from what you meant to say—like going from the blankets to the beans to the hymns—do you find it hard to come up with the actual words you need, or do the words come to you just fine but they just tumble out in the wrong order and you can't seem to stop yourself from saying all those other things?\n\nPatient: Oh, the words come to me just fine, Doctor. It's just exactly like you said, they come out but they just keep going and going and going, and I can't seem to rein them back in. \n\nI really do mean to answer straight! It was like the motor just cut out right in the middle of the job. I didn't decide to keep it up there. My body just froze up solid as a block of ice. And my mind, well, I was in there thinking, 'Put the spoon down, folks are waiting,' but my arm just wouldn't get the message. It was just stuck there in the air, heavy as lead.\n\nAnd then with those napkins... oh, my goodness, it wasn't that I felt I needed them to be perfect or anything like that. It was more like my hands just got caught on a loop, like a broken record playing the same skip over and over. I was just folding, and folding, and smoothing that same paper napkin—they buy them in bulk from the warehouse store now, not the nice soft ones we used to have back in the nineties, so they're rough on the hands—and my fingers were just doing it all on their own. I didn't decide to keep doing it. I just couldn't seem to make them stop and do the next thing, which was handing it to Mr. Henderson who was standing right there with his slice of cherry pie just looking at me like I'd lost my marbles. \n\nSo it's just like I told you, I keep doing these odd things at the potluck, just freezing up or repeating the same motion while folks are waiting on me, and it's not me deciding to do it at all. My body just gets entirely stuck.\n\nDoctor: When your arm was frozen holding the spoon up in the air, or when your hands were stuck folding those napkins, if someone had tapped you on the shoulder and said 'Stop, put it down right now,' do you think you could have forced yourself to stop and put the spoon down or put the napkins aside? Or would your body just not obey no matter how hard you tried?\n\nPatient: Well, that's just the thing of it, Doctor. See, when my arm was up in the air with that spoon—and like I said, it was a heavy one, one of those good sturdy metal ones we've had at the church since Reverend Thomas was there, oh, must be thirty years ago now—I was standing there, frozen stiff. And Mrs. Gable, she was right next to me serving the green beans. She did notice. She leaned over and she touched my arm, right here on the elbow, and she whispered, 'Mary, what on earth are you doing? Serve the macaroni.' \n\nAnd you know, I heard her clear as a bell. I wanted to put that spoon down. I was telling my arm, 'Put the spoon down, Mary, put it down right into the bowl.' But... it just wouldn't. It wouldn't obey me at all. No matter how hard I tried to force it, my arm just stayed locked up there in the air until it finally decided to come down on its own sweet time. \n\nAnd the same exact thing happened with the napkins. Mr. Henderson, bless his heart, he actually cleared his throat real loud, you know how men do when they're getting impatient, and he said, 'Mary, I just need a napkin for my pie.' He didn't tap my shoulder, but he spoke right to me, loud enough for the whole line to hear. And I tried, Doctor, I really did. I tried to just let go of that paper square and hand it over. But my fingers just kept right on smoothing and folding. It was like my brain was shouting 'stop' and my hands were completely deaf to it. So no, even with folks telling me to stop, I just couldn't make my body mind me. It's the most helpless feeling in the world, just being trapped inside yourself while everybody watches.\n\nDoctor: Mary, when did these freezing episodes and repetitive hand movements first start happening? Was it something that came on suddenly one day, or has it been gradually getting worse over weeks or months?\n\nPatient: Well, let me think on that a minute, Doctor. It certainly didn't just happen overnight, like somebody flipping a light switch, no sir. It's been... oh, I'd say right around six months now. Yes, because it was just about the time we were getting ready for the big Easter sunrise service. We always do a big breakfast after that, with the scrambled eggs and the sausage links. We don't use the patties because the links are just easier to keep warm in those metal chafing dishes they keep down in the church basement, you know, the ones with the little little fire cans underneath them. \n\nAnd that's when I first started noticing it, these little spells where my hands would just get stuck doing something odd, like I was telling you with the spoon and the napkins. But it's not just the freezing up, either, Doctor. Folks have been telling me for about that same six months that my talking has gotten all tangled up, too. They say I'm terribly hard to follow, that I just go on and on and they don't know what I'm trying to get at or what I mean. Like my sister-in-law Beatrice, she told me just the other day that she can't make heads or tails of what I'm saying half the time lately. And I don't mean to be confusing, I really don't, I just have so much on my mind and it all comes out at once, but apparently my talking has just been a mess since the spring. \n\nSo yes, I'd say it's been a good six months of this odd behavior and my talking being so hard for people to understand. Six whole months of just feeling like I'm not quite steering my own ship, and it just breaks my heart because I've always prided myself on being sharp as a tack when it comes to organizing the church meals, and now I'm just making a spectacle of myself.\n\nDoctor: Mary, besides the trouble with your speech that people have mentioned, have you noticed any changes in your memory, or do you find yourself having trouble with things like remembering names, dates, or keeping track of what you need to do during the day?\n\nPatient: Well, memory... yes, I suppose it is my memory, too. It's not just the names, though goodness knows I've known some of these folks since we were in pigtails and suddenly I look at them and just draw a complete blank. But mostly it's the plans, Doctor, keeping track of what I'm supposed to be doing during the week. It's gotten so bad that I've actually had to step back from my choir duties and a lot of my church volunteering. \n\nI used to handle the schedule for the choir robes, you see, making sure they got picked up and dropped off at the dry cleaners over on Elm Street—the one run by the Miller family, because they give the church a nice discount and they don't use that terrible heavy starch that makes the collars scratch your neck all through the sermon—but lately, I've just been getting all the plans completely mixed up. I'd forget which Sunday we needed the gold sashes and which was the purple, or I'd mix up the dates for the committee meetings and tell people the wrong time to show up, or I'd completely forget who was supposed to bring the communion bread. \n\nAnd it just... well, it makes folks uncomfortable. You can see it in their faces. They don't want to say anything harsh, bless their hearts, but I can tell they get real uneasy when I start getting the plans backwards or I show up on the wrong day entirely. And then poor Mrs. Higgins or somebody else has to come in right behind me and completely redo what I was supposed to handle in the first place. They have to make all the phone calls again and fix my messes just to make sure Sunday service goes off right. \n\nSo I just told Pastor Davis that I need to take a step back from the choir and the organizing for a while. It just hurts my pride, Doctor, it really does, having to give up my duties and watch other people redo my work just because I can't keep a simple plan straight in my head anymore.\n\nDoctor: Mary, have you noticed any weakness in your arms or legs, or do your muscles feel tight and stiff? And have you or anyone else noticed any twitching or rippling movements under your skin, especially in your arms, legs, or tongue?\n\nPatient: Well, weakness? No, Doctor, I can't say I've felt any weakness at all. My arms are still as strong as they ever were, praise the Lord. Just yesterday I was carrying in the groceries—two heavy paper sacks, mind you, because I don't like those flimsy plastic ones they use nowadays, they always tear right at the bottom the second you put canned goods in them, and I had three heavy cans of sliced peaches and a big tin of Maxwell House coffee in there—and I carried them right up the front steps without a lick of trouble. So my arms are just fine. And my legs, too. I walk down to the mailbox at the end of the driveway every single morning, rain or shine, and that's a good fifty yards down a gravel path, and my legs carry me just fine. \n\nAnd as for them feeling tight or stiff... well, no, not really. I mean, my knees might pop a little bit when I first get up out of my good armchair, the floral one in the living room that Arthur bought me for our anniversary years ago, but my muscles themselves aren't stiff or tight like you're asking. Now, when I freeze up like a statue, like I was telling you about with the spoon, well sure, I'm stuck then, but when I'm just going about my normal day and my body is listening to me, my muscles feel perfectly normal. \n\nAnd twitching? Rippling under the skin? Oh, goodness gracious, no! That sounds just awful, Doctor, like something out of one of those scary moving pictures my grandson likes to watch on the television, with bugs or something moving around inside a person. No, no, I haven't seen anything like that, and nobody else at the church or in my family has said a word about it either. My skin is just regular old lady skin, a bit thinner and more wrinkled than it used to be, maybe, but nothing is twitching or rippling underneath it, I can promise you that. \n\nAnd my tongue? No, no twitching there either. I know I told you my talking gets all tangled up and confusing for folks lately, but my tongue itself works just fine. It's not jumping around in my mouth or anything strange like that. I can still eat my peppermint hard candies and sip my hot tea without biting it or having it spasm on me. So no, Doctor, none of that twitching or weakness, none at all. It's just the freezing up and my mind getting all my plans mixed up that are giving me all this grief.\n\nDoctor: Mary, when you're talking and people say it's hard to understand you, do you have trouble finding the right words to say, or do you have trouble understanding what other people are saying to you?\n\nPatient: Well, now, let me think on that... no, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I understand folks perfectly fine. My hearing is still as sharp as it ever was, thank the Lord, and when somebody asks me a question, I know exactly what they're saying to me. And as for finding the words, oh goodness, I have plenty of words! Sometimes I think I have too many words all trying to get out the front door at the exact same time. \n\nIt’s more like... well, like just the other day. The ladies from the church auxiliary, they were asking me about the blankets we knit for the winter charity drive, or maybe it was about the schedule for choir practice, I forget which exactly, but I understood perfectly what they wanted to know. And I mean to answer them straight, I really do. I have the answer right there in my head. But when I open my mouth, my words just decide to take a walk all on their own. \n\nI'll start off trying to tell them about the yarn for the blankets, but then suddenly my words just run off and I'm talking about the green beans I was snapping on the porch that morning. Mr. Henderson brought over a whole bushel from his garden, you see, the nice Kentucky Wonders that are so good for canning. And then, before you know it, I'm not talking about beans anymore, I'm going on about the hymns we sang last Sunday—like \"How Great Thou Art,\" which is my absolute favorite, though the new piano player takes it at much too fast a tempo if you ask me—and from the hymns, I'm suddenly rambling all about my roses. I have these beautiful yellow climbing roses on the south side of the house, and they need so much pruning this time of year or they just take over the whole trellis. \n\nAnd I'll be talking and talking, going from the beans to the hymns to my roses, and I'll look up, and those poor ladies... they just have this look on their faces. Folks look at me like they completely lost the thread and they can't find what I'm saying at all. It's like they're searching for the answer about the blankets in all that chatter, and it's just gotten buried. So, no, I don't have trouble understanding them, and I know the words I want to use, but they just tumble out in this big, long river that doesn't go where it's supposed to.\n\nDoctor: Mary, before all of this started about six months ago—the freezing up, the trouble with your speech, and the memory problems—did you have any kind of head injury, fall, or accident? I never go down there in my stocking feet or those cheap little slippers they sell at the pharmacy, the ones with the smooth bottoms that just ask for a broken hip. I see ladies at the church doing that in their own homes and I just think, well, you're just inviting trouble. So no, I haven't taken any tumbles or hit my head, not once. \n\nAnd a stroke? Or some sudden sickness? No, thank the Lord. I've been right as rain in my body. I eat a good bowl of oatmeal every single morning—the real kind, mind you, not those little paper packets full of sugar and fake apples, but the slow-cooked oats on the stovetop—and I think that keeps a person strong. I haven't been to the hospital for anything sudden, haven't had any spells or strokes or anything of that nature. It's just... well, it's just this freezing up and my mind getting tangled like a ball of yarn that the cat got into. But before all this started up six months ago, no, I was perfectly fine. Not a single accident or sudden illness to speak of.\n\nDoctor: Mary, besides the freezing up and the trouble keeping your thoughts organized, have you noticed any changes in your personality or the way you act? For instance, do you find yourself doing things that are out of character for you, or acting in ways that your family or friends have said seem unlike the old Mary?\n\nPatient: Changes in how I act? Well, now, let me just picture it... it’s my whole self, really. Both sides exactly the same. It’s not like my right arm gets stuck and my left arm is free to wave hello. It's terribly frustrating, because the words are all perfectly good words, they just refuse to stay in the order I meant to put them in.\n\nDoctor: Mary, when you're trying to talk about something specific, like the choir practice that Mrs. Higgins asked you about, do you ever find yourself stuck searching for a particular word—like you know what you want to say but the word just won't come to you? Or does the word always come to you, it's just that other words and topics keep interrupting and pushing their way in?\n\nPatient: Well, exactly like I was just saying a moment ago, Doctor, I don't ever have to go digging around for a word. It's not like when you get older and you can't remember the name of the fella at the grocery store and you just stand there snapping your fingers trying to pull it out of thin air. No, no, my words are right there, clear as a bell. \n\nIt’s just... well, like I was telling you about my friends at the church. When the ladies ask me about the baby blankets or what time we're doing the choir practice, I really do mean to answer them straight as an arrow. I have the right word ready and waiting! But then it’s like a dam breaks, and all these other topics just push their way right to the front of the line. The words don't hide from me, they just... they run off entirely on their own. One minute I'm trying to say something simple, and the next my words are running off from the pressure-cooker beans straight to the Sunday hymns, and then right on over to my yellow roses and those awful Japanese beetles. \n\nThey just crowd in and interrupt what I meant to say, tumbling out so fast I can't catch them. And the worst part is, I can see it on everybody's faces. The ladies will just stand there, holding their purses or their casseroles, and they look at me like they absolutely cannot find what I'm saying. They get this confused little wrinkle right between their eyebrows, like I've started speaking Greek or something, when all I'm doing is talking about the garden! So I never lose the word I need, Doctor, I just get a hundred other ones I didn't ask for, all pushing their way out at the exact same time.\n\nDoctor: Mary, when people are talking to you—not you talking to them, but when they're speaking to you—do you find it easy to understand what they mean, or do you sometimes have trouble following along when someone uses complicated words or talks about something abstract or not so concrete?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, Doctor, I don't have any trouble understanding what people mean. I hear them clear as day and I know exactly what they're getting at. Now, I know I didn't get to finish high school—I had to leave school back in the eighth grade to help my mother with the younger ones, there were six of us kids, you see, and someone had to do the washing and the cooking—but that doesn't mean I don't have a good head on my shoulders. I understand complicated things just fine! \n\nWhy, just the other week, Pastor Thomas was giving this long, terribly complicated sermon about the metaphysical nature of grace—that was the exact word he used, metaphysical, which is a big ten-dollar word if you ask me—and he was going on and on about abstract concepts and the Holy Spirit and all sorts of deep theological things that would make some people's heads spin. But I followed every single word. I sat right there in the third pew, right next to Mrs. Higgins who was nodding off, bless her heart, and I understood exactly what he meant about grace being like a river that washes over the stones in a creek bed. \n\nAnd it's the exact same thing when I watch the evening news, with all those politicians in Washington using their fancy jargon and talking in circles about the economy and the infrastructure and whatnot. I know exactly what they're really saying, even when they try to dress it up in complicated words to confuse us everyday folks. I just sit in my armchair with my cross-stitch and I follow right along. So no, when folks talk to me, I don't get lost or confused at all. It's only my own words that run away from me and go off into the woods like I was telling you before, but my ears and my understanding work perfectly fine, always have.\n\nDoctor: Mary, I want to ask you something about how you've been feeling emotionally over these past six months. Have you noticed any changes in what makes you angry or upset? For instance, do you find yourself getting frustrated or irritable more easily than you used to, or have people at church mentioned that you seem different in your mood or temperament?\n\nPatient: Well, heavens no, Doctor, I haven't noticed anything like that at all. I've never been one to have a short temper, not now and not ever. My mother, God rest her soul, she used to say I was the most even-tempered out of all six of us kids. And you know, when you've got six children running around a little farmhouse and you're the one helping do all the washing and the cooking because you had to leave school early, well, if you're the sort to get mad easily, you'd just be mad from sunup to sundown! It’s that nice soft knit one I got on sale at JCPenney a few years back, the one with the little pearl buttons. \n\nNow, a lot of women would have pitched an absolute fit right then and there, having coffee spilled on their Sunday best, but I didn't get upset one bit. I didn't raise my voice or get irritable or snap at her. I just patted her arm and told her it was no use crying over spilled coffee, and I marched right into the ladies' room to dab it with some cold water and a paper towel before it could set into the fibers. \n\nSo, no, I don't find myself getting frustrated or angry more easily these last six months. I might get frustrated with my own words when they won't line up, or maybe with those Japanese beetles tearing up my yellow roses, I'll give you that, because they are just a menace this year... but with people and just my everyday feelings? No, my mood is just as cheerful and steady as it's always been. So, you see, I haven't paid much mind to my habits at home, but I came here because I keep doing these odd things at church, like standing by the potluck table holding the serving spoon up and not moving, or folding that same stack of napkins over and over while people are just standing there waiting on me.
